title: Tuning the brain from the outside in: a new way forward for treating mental health disorders and beyond
text:
Dysfunction within the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex has been implicated in a large breadth of
brain disorders with psychiatric underpinnings. Targeting neuromodulation using focused
ultrasound in lieu of ablative strategies to this region holds promise as an important therapeutic
strategy, but substantial optimization is needed to make this a viable treatment. In addition, the
serendipitous adjacency of the dorsal anterior cingulate to the centrally located inferior sagittal
sinus provides an incredible opportunity to leverage this anatomical relationship to develop an
incisionless, intravascular ultrasound device-based strategy from bench to bedside.

title: Targeting deubiquitinase OTUD7A as a novel therapeutic strategy for Ewing sarcoma
text:
Ewing sarcoma is a rare and aggressive pediatric cancer of the bones or soft tissues and ~50% of patients
eventually relapse and die of the disease due to developed therapy resistance even with intensive multimodality
therapy, thus there is an urgent need for new targeted therapies. Recently, we found both genetic deletion and
pharmacological inhibition of deubiquitinase OTUD7A diminished Ewing sarcoma growth, providing a novel
therapeutic target for treating Ewing Sarcoma. This research aims to develop potent and selective OTUD7A
inhibitors suitable for clinical application and as such, may have a direct impact on outcomes and/or quality of
life for patients with Ewing sarcoma.

title: The Thromboxane-Prostanoid Receptor in Radiation-Induced Pulmonary Fibrosis
text:
Our preliminary data suggests that radiation induced pulmonary fibrosis (RIPF) is caused by radiation-induced
isoprostane signaling through the thromboxane-prostanoid receptor (TPr), and that blocking TPr with a small
molecule, ifetroban, significantly reduces RIPF. In this project, we test mechanistic hypotheses, ensure that
ifetroban does not diminish the effect of standard of care (immune checkpoint therapy), and still works to
reduce RIPF when combined with it. We also examine human radiation oncology patients to ensure that the
increased isoprostanes are also present in patients.

title: Molecular Imaging of the Immune-Suppressive TME in Prostate Cancer
text:
Prostate cancer (PCa) is the second leading cause of death from cancer in men in the U.S., with most men
succumbing to metastatic castration-resistant disease. Although treatment with immune checkpoints inhibitors
has had unprecedented responses in turning some deadly cancers into chronic diseases, 80% of cancers
including PCa have complex tumor microenvironments (TMEs) that are resistant to immune checkpoint
inhibitors. Our purpose in this application is to apply molecular and functional imaging to understand the role of
the TME, including hypoxia, metabolism, fibroblasts and the extracellular matrix (ECM), in creating an immune
suppressive and metastasis permissive TME that can, in the future, lead to treatments to induce an immune
reactive TME responsive to cancer immunotherapy to reduce mortality from PCa.

title: Self-Assembled Multifunctional Biointerfaces
text:
Controlling the properties of biomedical interfaces is critical for studying, diagnosing, and treating disease. This
research program aims to develop a versatile platform based on interfacial protein self-assembly for increasing
the functionality of biomedical and biological surfaces. Proof-of-concept projects explored in the proposed work
include enhancing nerve tissue repair using coatings with temporally orchestrated growth factor release,
improving the long-term performance of biosensors, and engineering live cell surfaces to control cell fate in
therapeutic applications.

title: Admin Core
text: The Administrative Core (AC) has been critical to the continued success of the Boston Area NORC over the last cycle. The NORC has continued to fill major gaps in the promotion of nutrition and obesity research in Boston. The AC facilitates the continued expansion of the NORC, leveraging a strong membership, including an increased number of junior investigators, accomplished in research across the translational spectrum, building a strong clinical and translational focus, and developing state of the art core services, including genomic and single cell transcriptomic techniques, cell culture and organoid services, mitochondrial functional assessment, model development, detailed metabolic assessment in animal models, and highly sophisticated functional imaging techniques allowing investigators to probe human metabolic pathways including appetite, substrate flux, and tissue specific inflammation. The goals of the Boston Area NORC AC are: 1) to provide an overall organizational structure with which to direct the NORC, including a Director experienced in clinical and translational research and 4 strong Associate Directors (AD’s) with complimentary expertise; 2) to capitalize on a strong Research Base in Nutrition and Obesity in Boston, with themes in translational research; 3) To foster cutting edge research by enabling highly successful and well used cores: Genomics and Cell Biology (GCB), Metabolic Phenotyping (MP) and Metabolic Imaging (MIC) cores, leveraging the strengths in these areas (including functional adipose imaging, PET and Functional Neuroimaging (MI); and Metabolomics, Mitochondrial Function, Adipocyte Biology, and Model Development (MP), next generation sequencing, single-cell profiling, high-content/high-throughout cell- based assays, cell culture and organoids, and bioinformatics (GCB) demonstrating significant usage and facilitating key publications; 4) To administer a vibrant P&F Program which has been a highly successful component of the NORC fostering promotion of successful young scientists in the nutrition/obesity field, leveraging pilot funds into significant NIH grant support, and catalyzing new collaborations in translational science. 5) To administer a highly respected and popular enrichment program, including an Annual Symposium on nutrition and obesity topics, responsive to changing research priorities, training the next generation of scientists in nutrition and metabolism through coursework, and mentoring of young trainees, via our annual P&F Symposium; 6) To promote the advancement of early career researchers in nutrition and obesity research, through funding an RFA and ongoing efforts to increase P&F applications and success rates for early career researchers.

title: J-domain protein conformational selectivity for tau in disease
text:
Molecular chaperones are proteins that help other proteins adopt proper shapes. When chaperones fail to
function proteins can adopt improper shapes that can cause human diseases including Alzheimer’s. We aim to
understand how molecular chaperones regulate the formation of improper protein shapes and leverage this
information to develop novel therapies that prevent the formation of disease-forming protein conformations.

title: Elucidating the role of an essential transcription factor in SWI/SNF -mutant rhabdoid tumors
text:
Mutations in chromatin regulatory genes frequently cause cancer. This is true of the highly lethal childhood
rhabdoid tumor, which is caused by the loss of SMARCB1, a subunit of the SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling
complex. I have discovered that the disruption of a normally inconsequential transcription factor kills rhabdoid
tumor cells and I aim to investigate why this occurs and whether this finding can be leveraged as a therapeutic
opportunity for SMARCB1-deficient cancers.

title: Flow Cytometry and Cellular Imaging Core Facility (FCCIF)
text: FLOW CYTOMETRY AND CELLULAR IMAGING FACILITY (FCCIF) The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center (MD Anderson) Flow Cytometry and Cellular Imaging Facility (FCCIF) offers a suite of leading-edge single cell analysis services. The aims of the FCCIF are 1) to provide the MD Anderson research community with unparalleled expertise to address important research hypotheses using robust, state-of-the-art flow cytometry and cellular imaging techniques; 2) to develop and validate innovative methods in the fields of cytometry, cell sorting, and cellular imaging; and 3) to train users in applicable methodology and best practices in data collection and analysis to facilitate research rigor and reproducibility. FCCIF has strategic laboratory locations at North Campus, South Campus, and at the Oncology Research and Immuno-mONitoring (ORION) clinical building site, which facilitate collaborations and offer a complete range of services and ~40 instruments for researchers. North Campus services include flow cytometry (spectral and conventional), cell sorting (spectral and conventional), confocal and multi-spectral imaging, live cell and digital microscopy, sequential ImmunoFluorescence (seqIF), cytometry by time-of-flight (CyTOF) suspension mass cytometry, and CyTOF imaging mass cytometry. The South Campus site provides access to state-of-the-art flow cytometry (spectral and conventional) and cell sorting (spectral and conventional) for sophisticated multi-parametric single cell analysis. The ORION facility offers select instruments for multiplexing, flow cytometry, and immunoassays of clinical samples. FCCIF equips investigators with the latest tools and instruments in a collaborative environment, presents structured training and education opportunities, offers innovative assay design consultations, and provides analysis support tailored for specific research needs. During 2024, the FCCIF supported 233 Cancer Center members from all nine programs (81% of user base), reflecting the critical importance of FCCIF services to members. Furthermore, in 2024, FCCIF supported 133 publications (55% in high-impact journals (Journal Impact Factor ≥10)) and facilitated 429 peer-reviewed grants awarded to members. Future plans include the continued development of high-content assays with a specific focus on spatial multiomics to meet high-throughput demands. FCCIF will expand by offering analytical modalities of 3D organoid and 3D engineered tissues in response to the NIH initiative that prioritizes new approaches and methods for human-based research. It will increase its servicing capacity with new equipment and staff to continue delivering state-of-the-art services and increase collaborations with investigators. New staff will be crucial for providing more high-plex immuno-phenotyping, high-plex imaging, spatial analysis services, and keeping up with increased investigator requests.

title: Shared Mechanisms of Tau Toxicity Among Neurodegenerative Diseases
text:
Abnormality of tau is a common pathological feature of neurodegenerative diseases collectively known
as tauopathies. There is also overwhelming evidence implicating defects in mitochondria and
especially mitochondrial complex I in the pathogenesis of these diseases. This project will test a novel
mechanism by which pathogenic tau and mitochondrial complex I dysfunction are connected and thus
has the potential to offer new therapeutic strategies for a broad spectrum of neurodegenerative
diseases, including Alzheimer's disease and Alzheimer's disease related dementias (AD/ADRD), for
which there is currently no effective treatment.

title: Discovery of osteoblast and osteoclast bone mass effector genes using advanced genomics
text:
Genome wide association studies (GWAS) have revolutionized the field of complex disease genetics. Intense
efforts by large-scale international collaborations, including ours, have been successful in discovering key
genetic variants robustly associated with bone mineral density (BMD) and fracture; however, GWAS only
reports genomic signals associated with a given trait and does not necessarily identify culprit effector genes.
Given the need for `variant to gene mapping', plus the need to expand the collection of public domain genomic
data relevant to bone, we will build on our initial published results by utilizing our multi-step genomic analysis
pathway and functional follow-up using siRNA and CRISPR in osteoblasts and osteoclasts and knockout
mouse models to pinpoint causal gene(s) at key BMD and fracture GWAS-implicated locus.

title: Helicobacter Infection and Liver Cancer Risk among African Americans and Whites in the United States
text: Project Narrative This proposal will provide the most comprehensive study to date of H. pylori, other Helicobacter infection and liver cancer in both African Americans (AAs) and whites by using a pooled nested case-control study. Results from this proposal have etiologic relevance and clinical impact by identifying (1) a novel bacterial infection for non-viral liver cancer; and (2) race/ethnic-specific Helicobacter infection associated with liver cancer that will inform designing interventions to reduce existing disparities, given the high prevalence of H. pylori infection in AAs in the U.S. These investigations into the associations between bacterial infections and liver cancer risk will also advance the field of liver cancer etiology, prevention, and case management.

title: Validation and implementation of ctDNA as a clinically informative biomarkerin AYAs with sarcomas.
text:
Adolescents and young adults with sarcomas suffer a significant burden of morbidity and mortality with minimal
improvements in outcomes in recent decades. The presence of metastatic disease remains the only strong
prognostic factor, and biomarkers are needed to inform new approaches to testing risk-stratified therapy. In the
proposed study, I will determine prognostic thresholds for ctDNA burden for fusion-positive and fusion negative
sarcomas leveraging structural features seen across all sarcomas and then assess the impact of clinical ctDNA
testing for post-treatment surveillance in Ewing sarcoma.

title: Development of the High-Density SNAP-Dimer Microarray for Functional Analysis of Dimeric Protein Complexes
text:
Development of the High-Density SNAP-Dimer Microarray for Functional Analysis of Dimeric Protein
Complexes
 Opportunity Number: PA-24-245
 PIs: Mary S. Ozers and Christopher L. Warren
Most drugs target only a small portion of proteins involved in disease, with most druggable pockets already
exhausted and many crucial protein-protein interactions untapped. This project aims to develop the SNAP-
Dimer protein microarray as a groundbreaking tool to study how pairs of proteins, like those involved in
metastatic breast cancer, interact and respond to drugs. By focusing on challenging targets like estrogen
receptor-alpha, this innovative approach could facilitate new treatments for diseases that currently have limited
options.

title: Inflammatory and Genetic Cardiomyopathies: Metabolic Phenotyping to Guide Diagnosis and Therapy
text:
Many patients with the combination of structural heart disease and heart rhythm disorders have either a
genetic cause or inflammatory cause (immune system attacking the heart), but these can be challenging to
diagnose. This proposal systematically studies such patients with genetic testing, advanced cardiac imaging,
blood-based studies of metabolism and heart tissue biopsy with next-generation histology/pathology methods
to help create new diagnostic tests. Correctly diagnosing these patients will help clinicians not only provide
necessary treatment, but also stop unnecessary immunosuppression, and refer patients’ family members for
“cascade” genetic testing when necessary; and a parallel mouse study utilizing genetic models of heart
disease will allow study of novel therapies for these conditions.

title: The first adaptable 3D-formfitting microelectrode array for organoid-based models of neurological and neurodegenerative diseases
text:
Brain organoids replicate critical organ and tissue-specific features not observed in animal models or 2D cell
cultures to model human organ structure and function under healthy and disease conditions. A major limitation
for the utility of brain organoids for pre-clinical drug development is the lack of adequate instrumentation to
monitor spatial and temporal neural network organization across the surface of physiologically intact organoids.
The proposed 3D model platform will solve this problem, thus improving the efficacy to assess drug candidates
in pre-clinical research to treat neurological and neurodegenerative diseases.

title: Nonparametric Methods to Address Scientific Questions in Aging Integrating Real-World and Research Databases
text:
Routinely-collected data in electronic health records (EHRs) have the potential to rapidly drive innovations in
healthcare, particularly in areas where traditional studies are infeasible, but are prone to errors introduced in
the data extraction process. Correcting errors and addressing missing data in these data sources ensures that
downstream statistical inferences will provide reliable clinical evidence for improved health and healthcare
delivery. We will create novel statistical methods and study designs, drawing on tools from machine learning
and survey statistics, to robustly and efficiently handle error-prone routine EHR data to estimate causal
inference estimands and prediction model performance; we illustrate these methods in a case study that
develops and evaluates risk prediction models for advanced age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and the
association between advanced AMD risk and Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias (ADRD).

title: Investigating the Mechanisms and Impact of Amyloid-Beta Mediated Disruption of Synaptic Nanoachitecture
text:
Alzheimer’s Disease (AD) is a significant global health crisis, affecting approximately 55 million people
worldwide, and around 6.7 million individuals in the United States alone. This disease causes dementia, memory
loss and cognitive decline, and entails the disruption of the communication between brain cells, neurons, at small
structures called synapses, by Amyloid-Beta, one of several proteins of interest frequently researched in context
of AD. This research aims to uncover how a recently described phenomenon, whereby the nano-scale
organization of specific synaptic proteins is disrupted by Amyloid-Beta, might underlie previously researched
disruptions to synaptic activity, and the loss of synapses.

title: Deciphering the Role of Reductive Stress in Non Small Cell Lung Cancer
text:
The NRF2 transcription factor orchestrates cellular anti-oxidant response, promoting a reductive environment
that is generally required for unchecked proliferation. Surprisingly, in ~16% of non small cell lung cancer
(NSCLC) cell lines, NRF2 activation leads to a severe block in growth resulting from a decrease in mitochondrial
metabolism and electron transport chain dysfunction. The goal of this application is to use a suite of advanced
metabolomic, chemical-proteomic and genomic technologies to understand how the NRF2 regulated cellular
environment is detrimental to cell proliferation and to test the efficacy of activating NRF2 in vivo to block NSCLC
growth.

title: Mechanisms underlying USP1-mediated bypass of EWS-FLI1 oncogene-induced replication stress in Ewing sarcoma
text:
EWS-FLI1 oncogenic transcription factor regulates the expression of USP1 in Ewing sarcoma, an aggressive
pediatric bone cancer. USP1 deubiquitinase regulates HELLS and is required for stem cell maintenance, genome
stability and promotes cell proliferation bypassing oncogene-induced replication stress.
